name: Gamboge Yellow
lede: Gamboge is the bright, slightly lemony yellow of a Southeast Asian tree resin, named for Cambodia, a watercolor of the East India trade and, for a few weeks in 1908, the proof that atoms exist.

sections.title: A name from Cambodia
sections.body:
*Gamboge* is a corruption of the old name for Cambodia, and the pigment is the resin of trees that grow there and in neighboring countries [1][2][4]. The word passed through *cambodiam*, *camboja* and *camboge* before settling into English, and older books also spell it *gumboge* and *gutti*, the last from a Malay word for gum [1]. Paterson defines it as a strong, reddish yellow [5].

Strictly it is a resin and not a gum, so the old trade name *cadie gum* was always a misnomer [1]. Chinese painters call the pigment *teng huang*, rattan yellow, though Finlay was also told ivy yellow, and it comes from neither plant [1][2]. The Japanese reading of the same characters, *to-o*, has been translated as wisteria yellow [1]. The English adjective *gambogious* was invented by Ivor Brown in 1973 in praise of the flamboyance of the word [5]. In a synesthesia survey that Birren quotes from Galton, one respondent saw the vowel I as gamboge, a light bright yellow, though family members disagreed [12].

sections.title: From tree to pipe
sections.body:
The main source is *Garcinia hanburyi*, a tall tree related to the mangosteen, and its resin is sold as Siam gamboge [1][2]. Other species give other grades: *G. morella* supplies the Ceylon kind, and further relatives grow in India, Sri Lanka and Myanmar [1].

Harvesting is slow. The collector makes a deep cut in the trunk, sets a hollowed length of bamboo beneath it, and does not come back until the following year [2]. St Clair gives the same picture, with trees at least a decade old and a year or more to fill a bamboo [3]. Coles adds that the resin is roasted over a fire to drive off moisture before the solid cylinder is removed [6]. The tubes of hardened resin, which is how it was sold, are called pipe gamboge [1].

In that hardened state the resin is a dull brownish red [1]. It turns brilliant yellow once it meets water [2][3]. Finlay's Hong Kong supplier touched a wet brush to a brown lump and released a yellow so bright she called it almost fluorescent [2]. St Clair writes the same of a toffee-brown cake and a drop of water [3].

sections.title: Eight centuries in Asia
sections.body:
Gamboge has been used in Chinese and Japanese painting since at least the eighth century [2][4]. Winter lists Japanese occurrences from the eighth through the nineteenth centuries, and the pigment has been found beneath the gold paint of wall paintings at the Maitepnimit Temple in Thailand [1]. Finlay adds that it was probably sometimes used on early Indian miniatures to paint Krishna's yellow clothes [2].

It was always imported, because the trees grow only in tropical forests of South-East Asia [2][1]. Early European use has been tentatively identified in an Armenian gospel of about 1300, though the Compendium treats that as uncertain [1].

The first arrivals in Europe are reported differently [4][3]. Ball and St Clair both date regular imports by the British East India Company to 1615, and Paterson puts its English use at the start of the seventeenth century [4][3][5]. St Clair also reports a first cargo in the hull of a Dutch trading ship in 1603 [3]. The books do not say whether the 1603 cargo was a one-off [3].

sections.title: Into the European paint box
sections.body:
Europeans met gamboge as medicine before they met it as paint. Druggists sold it as a purgative, and this is reported to have helped its importation [4]. Robert Christison in 1836 called it an excellent and powerful purgative, and workers who crushed it at Winsor & Newton had to leave the room hourly [3].

Painters took it up anyway. Its properties suit watercolor better than oil, though it turns up in some oils, notably those of early Flemish painters, who were well placed to benefit from the Dutch trade [4]. [[painter:rembrandt-van-rijn|Rembrandt]] favored it in oil for the golden halos around his figures, by St Clair's account, and Ball says the resin takes on a golden hue in oil [3][4]. The Compendium cautions that a Dresden Rembrandt identification was noted and not authenticated, and it calls proven finds of gamboge in art scarce and often vague [1].

Turner's watercolor box held gamboge, and so did Reynolds's palette [1][3]. Gilchrist's list of William Blake's few pigments includes occasional gamboge among the vermilion and ultramarine [8]. Mayerne and Smith recommended it as a watercolor in the seventeenth century, and it was used for tinting prints [1].

sections.title: The yellow that defined other yellows
sections.body:
In the colors of Werner's mineral nomenclature, as extended by Patrick Syme in 1821, gamboge yellow stands as the standard of the yellow series [7]. Werner's own characteristic yellow, lemon yellow, turned out to be gamboge yellow with a touch of ash grey, so it could not serve as the standard [7]. Syme then wrote the other yellows as recipes with gamboge in them. Primrose yellow is gamboge with a little sulphur yellow and much white [7]. King's yellow is gamboge with a small portion of saffron yellow, and saffron yellow is gamboge with gallstone yellow in about equal parts [7]. Compare [[flower:saffron|saffron]] and [[gallstone-yellow]].

The oranges and greens are built the same way. Dutch orange is gamboge with carmine, orpiment orange is gamboge and arterial blood red in about equal parts, and scarlet red is arterial blood red with a little gamboge [7]. Emerald green is about equal parts Berlin blue and gamboge yellow, and duck green adds indigo, more gamboge and a very little carmine [7]. See [[orpiment-orange]] and [[emerald-green]].

Syme took the name from painters' paint boxes. Baty notes that gamboge yellow, Sienna yellow, sap green, lake red and umber brown were all pigment names he borrowed [7]. For the natural examples of gamboge yellow, Syme gave the wings of the goldfinch and the canary, the yellow jasmine and a high-colored sulphur [7]. Our library records Gamboge Yellow from Syme's Werner numbers 66 and 67, which is its earliest dated source in our data [14].

sections.title: A primary yellow, and a green
sections.body:
Several color theorists made gamboge their primary yellow [8]. Pfannenschmidt's sets of 1792 used carmine, gamboge and natural ultramarine, and Sowerby chose gamboge, carmine and Prussian blue [8]. In the 1790s Lamarck proposed ultramarine, carmine and gamboge, noting that gamboge, though less close to the spectral yellow than orpiment, could be mixed with lead white without harm [8]. Ogden Rood's *Modern Chromatics* of 1879 later drew its contrast diagrams with real pigments, among them ultramarine, emerald green, vermilion and gamboge [17].

Painters mixed it with blue for greens. A chart of permanent colors of 1816 recommends indigo mixed with gamboge for the green of trees [13]. Gamboge and Prussian blue make Hooker's green, which Ball calls an eighteenth-century watercolor and which St Clair ties to the botanical artist William Hooker (1779 to 1832) [4][3]. The books therefore disagree about when it dates. For the blue half of that green, see [[prussian-blue]].

sections.title: The yellow that counted atoms
sections.body: The most surprising use of gamboge was in a physics laboratory. In 1908 the French physicist Jean Perrin suspended tiny gamboge particles in water and watched them jiggle, a demonstration of Brownian motion and so evidence for atoms [3][4]. St Clair gives the depth of his shallow layers as 0.005 inch and says the particles were still moving days later [3]. Perrin won the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for the work [3]. St Clair suggests that scientists were already familiar with the resin because it was a drug [3].

sections.title: Fading, adulteration and war
sections.body:
Gamboge fades. Ball says it goes rapidly in bright light, and Gurney lists it among the historic pigments not sufficiently lightfast [4][9]. The nineteenth-century replacement was aureolin, a cobalt yellow, though the books give different dates: Paterson says 1851, Ball says aureolin was synthesized in 1831 and first marketed in 1861 [5][4]. St Clair adds that aureolin was less bright and translucent than gamboge but less prone to fading [3]. Pastoureau, for the record, calls gamboge solid, bright and unsaturated; by his usage that seems to mean durable, which the other books contradict [10].

Adulteration was common. Winter reports pine resin, starch and even sand, rice meal and dextrin mixed into the resin, with lead chromate added to correct the color after starch dulled it [1]. In wartime the supply worsened. Finlay's supplier said that it gets mixed with mud in wartime, and that people could be killed for gamboge because of landmines [2].

Winsor & Newton received parcels from Cambodia and possibly Vietnam in the 1970s and 1980s that contained exploded bullets, five of which sit in its technical director's office [2]. St Clair attributes the bullets to the Khmer Rouge period [3]. The company stopped selling gamboge in 2005, by St Clair's account, although Finlay describes it as still sold [3][2].

sections.title: Gamboge and the Indian yellow story
sections.body: Ball and Finlay discuss gamboge next to [[indian-yellow]], which reached Europe at about the same time and resembled it [4][2][3]. Ball repeats the story that Indian yellow was made from the urine of cows fed on mango leaves, and that it was outlawed by 1890 for cruelty [4]. That tale is unverified, and Finlay herself wonders aloud whether it is a joke at the visitor's expense [2]. Gurney's list says only that the pigment was *supposedly* made this way [9]. Nothing like it applies to gamboge, which is simply tree resin [1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here, #E6D058, is a clear lemony yellow [14]. It is lighter and greener than the pigment as most books describe it: Paterson calls gamboge reddish yellow and Jarman says it leans toward orange [5][11]. Our library takes its color from Werner's number 66, an aged and approximate swatch, and the nearest ISCC-NBS category is "brilliant yellow" [14]. In a real pipe the resin is brown, and the yellow appears only with water [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Gamboge Yellow is moderately common in our archive [15]. A color within four units of the swatch covers at least one per cent of the canvas in 111 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.47 per cent, which is more than 60 per cent of the named colors manage [15]. Inside a painting it is almost always a highlight, in 98 per cent of the cases we measured under the six-unit, five-per-cent test [15].

The strongest surprise is the Kalighat school of Calcutta [15]. Ten of 96 Kalighat works in the archive carry the color, about 10 per cent against 0.2 per cent for the archive as a whole [15]. The countries tell the same story: 15 of 721 Indian works, nearly 11 times the base rate [15]. These are look-alike hues in aged photographs and not a pigment test, so the match does not show that Kalighat painters used gamboge [15].

[[painter:pierre-bonnard|Bonnard]] is the most devoted painter, with the color in 5 of his 45 works here, 6.8 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [15]. The archive's decade of greatest concentration is the 1890s, with 13 of 1,173 works, or 5.7 times the expected rate [15]. The earliest painting in the data is Fra Angelico's *Coronation of the Virgin* of 1434, but the early centuries are thin and the match comes 387 years before the name's first record, so treat it as a coincidence of hue [15].

In print, *gamboge* peaks in Google Books around 1838 and has fallen to about 3 per cent of that peak by the 2000s [16]. The phrase *gamboge yellow* peaks in the 1850s and rose fastest in the 1820s [16]. Look for the color in a bright accent, a lemony sleeve or a halo, and ask whether the yellow sits in the highlight.

origin.named_after: Camboja, the old name for Cambodia, where the resin is chiefly gathered
origin.first_recorded: in use in Asian painting from the 8th century; imported to England from about 1615; Syme's Werner 1821 for the color name
origin.source: Pigment Compendium, "Gamboge"; Ball, Bright Earth, ch. 6
